claim: The Notch pathway is integrated into numerous developmental processes.
source: The Notch pathway is integrated into numerous developmental processes and therefore is fine-tuned on many levels, including receptor production, endocytosis, and degradation.
evidence: This is stated as established background information in the abstract.

claim: The Notch pathway is fine-tuned on many levels, including receptor production, endocytosis, and degradation.
source: The Notch pathway is integrated into numerous developmental processes and therefore is fine-tuned on many levels, including receptor production, endocytosis, and degradation.
evidence: This is stated as established background information in the abstract.

claim: Ligands from opposing cells (trans-ligands) activate Notch.
source: Notch is further characterized by a twofold relationship with its Delta-Serrate (DSL) ligands, as ligands from opposing cells (trans-ligands) activate Notch, whereas ligands expressed in the same cell (cis-ligands) inhibit signaling.
evidence: This is stated as established background information in the abstract.

claim: Ligands expressed in the same cell (cis-ligands) inhibit Notch signaling.
source: Notch is further characterized by a twofold relationship with its Delta-Serrate (DSL) ligands, as ligands from opposing cells (trans-ligands) activate Notch, whereas ligands expressed in the same cell (cis-ligands) inhibit signaling.
evidence: This is stated as established background information in the abstract.

claim: Cells without both cis- and trans-ligands can mediate Notch-dependent developmental events during Drosophila oogenesis.
source: We show that cells without both cis- and trans-ligands can mediate Notch-dependent developmental events during Drosophila oogenesis, indicating ligand-independent Notch activity occurs when the receptor is free of cis- and trans-ligands.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Ligand-independent Notch activity occurs when the receptor is free of cis- and trans-ligands.
source: We show that cells without both cis- and trans-ligands can mediate Notch-dependent developmental events during Drosophila oogenesis, indicating ligand-independent Notch activity occurs when the receptor is free of cis- and trans-ligands.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Cis-ligands can reduce Notch activity in endogenous and genetically induced situations of elevated trans-ligand-independent Notch signaling.
source: Furthermore, cis-ligands can reduce Notch activity in endogenous and genetically induced situations of elevated trans-ligand-independent Notch signaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Cis-expressed ligands exert their repressive effect on Notch signaling in cases of trans-ligand-independent activation.
source: We conclude that cis-expressed ligands exert their repressive effect on Notch signaling in cases of trans-ligand-independent activation, and propose a new function of cis-inhibition which buffers cells against accidental Notch activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Cis-inhibition buffers cells against accidental Notch activity.
source: We conclude that cis-expressed ligands exert their repressive effect on Notch signaling in cases of trans-ligand-independent activation, and propose a new function of cis-inhibition which buffers cells against accidental Notch activity.
evidence: This is a proposed function based on the experimental findings.

claim: Canonical Notch signaling begins when the Notch receptor receives a stimulus from a DSL-type ligand in an adjacent cell.
source: Canonical Notch signaling begins when the Notch receptor receives a stimulus from a DSL-type ligand (Delta [Dl] or Serrate [Ser] in Drosophila) in an adjacent cell, which leads to γ-secretase-dependent cleavage of Notch, and translocation of the intracellular domain—NICD— into the nucleus to act as a transcriptional co-activator (de Celis, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Canonical Notch signaling leads to γ-secretase-dependent cleavage of Notch.
source: Canonical Notch signaling begins when the Notch receptor receives a stimulus from a DSL-type ligand (Delta [Dl] or Serrate [Ser] in Drosophila) in an adjacent cell, which leads to γ-secretase-dependent cleavage of Notch, and translocation of the intracellular domain—NICD— into the nucleus to act as a transcriptional co-activator (de Celis, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Canonical Notch signaling leads to translocation of the intracellular domain (NICD) into the nucleus to act as a transcriptional co-activator.
source: Canonical Notch signaling begins when the Notch receptor receives a stimulus from a DSL-type ligand (Delta [Dl] or Serrate [Ser] in Drosophila) in an adjacent cell, which leads to γ-secretase-dependent cleavage of Notch, and translocation of the intracellular domain—NICD— into the nucleus to act as a transcriptional co-activator (de Celis, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Notch may be activated in a non-canonical, DSL-ligand independent manner.
source: Notch may also be activated in a non-canonical, DSL-ligand independent manner (Hori et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: DSL ligands can cis-inhibit ligand-dependent Notch activation when expressed in the same cell as the receptor.
source: DSL ligands can cis-inhibit ligand-dependent Notch activation when expressed in the same cell as the receptor (Micchelli et al., 1997; Del Álamo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The possibility of a relationship between DSL-ligand independent Notch activation and cis-expressed ligands has not been explored.
source: However, the possibility of a relationship between DSL-ligand independent Notch activation and cis-expressed ligands has not been explored.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: Dl is the sole signaling source in the developing Drosophila egg chamber.
source: The developing Drosophila egg chamber is a convenient model for dissecting the effects of Notch ligands in cis and in trans, as Dl is the sole signaling source and the signal sending and receiving cells can be easily distinguished (Deng et al., 2001; López-Schier and St Johnston, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the developing Drosophila egg chamber, the signal sending and receiving cells can be easily distinguished.
source: The developing Drosophila egg chamber is a convenient model for dissecting the effects of Notch ligands in cis and in trans, as Dl is the sole signaling source and the signal sending and receiving cells can be easily distinguished (Deng et al., 2001; López-Schier and St Johnston, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: At oogenesis stage 7, Notch signaling is activated in the somatic follicle cells by a robust germline Dl upregulation.
source: At oogenesis stage 7, Notch signaling is activated in the somatic follicle cells by a robust germline Dl upregulation, which leads to the expression of Hindsight (Hnt), downregulation of Cut, and the polyploidization of the follicle cells (Deng et al., 2001; López-Schier and St Johnston, 2001; Sun and Deng, 2005, 2007) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Notch signaling activation at oogenesis stage 7 leads to the expression of Hindsight (Hnt).
source: At oogenesis stage 7, Notch signaling is activated in the somatic follicle cells by a robust germline Dl upregulation, which leads to the expression of Hindsight (Hnt), downregulation of Cut, and the polyploidization of the follicle cells (Deng et al., 2001; López-Schier and St Johnston, 2001; Sun and Deng, 2005, 2007) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Notch signaling activation at oogenesis stage 7 leads to downregulation of Cut.
source: At oogenesis stage 7, Notch signaling is activated in the somatic follicle cells by a robust germline Dl upregulation, which leads to the expression of Hindsight (Hnt), downregulation of Cut, and the polyploidization of the follicle cells (Deng et al., 2001; López-Schier and St Johnston, 2001; Sun and Deng, 2005, 2007) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Notch signaling activation at oogenesis stage 7 leads to the polyploidization of the follicle cells.
source: At oogenesis stage 7, Notch signaling is activated in the somatic follicle cells by a robust germline Dl upregulation, which leads to the expression of Hindsight (Hnt), downregulation of Cut, and the polyploidization of the follicle cells (Deng et al., 2001; López-Schier and St Johnston, 2001; Sun and Deng, 2005, 2007) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: When Dl germline mutant clones were generated, the follicle cells failed to downregulate Cut expression, which persisted past stage 7.
source: When Dl germline mutant clones were generated (i.e., trans-activation was removed), the follicle cells failed to downregulate Cut expression, which persisted past stage 7, indicative of a failure to activate Notch (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Persistent Cut expression past stage 7 in Dl germline mutant clones is indicative of a failure to activate Notch.
source: When Dl germline mutant clones were generated (i.e., trans-activation was removed), the follicle cells failed to downregulate Cut expression, which persisted past stage 7, indicative of a failure to activate Notch (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Dl follicle cell mutant clones show precocious Cut downregulation at stage 6.
source: In contrast, Dl follicle cell mutant clones show precocious Cut downregulation at stage 6 attributable to the relief of cis-inhibition (Poulton et al., 2011) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 1C and supported by a citation.

claim: Precocious Cut downregulation at stage 6 in Dl follicle cell mutant clones is attributable to the relief of cis-inhibition.
source: In contrast, Dl follicle cell mutant clones show precocious Cut downregulation at stage 6 attributable to the relief of cis-inhibition (Poulton et al., 2011) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by a citation and experimental data in Figure 1C.

claim: Dl mutant clones in the follicle cells bordering Dl mutant clones in the germline (Dl-/Dl- cells) show correct Hnt and Cut expression from stage 7.
source: Surprisingly, Dl mutant clones in the follicle cells bordering Dl mutant clones in the germline (i.e., a germline with no signaling source, herein referred to as Dl-/Dl- cells) show correct Hnt and Cut expression from stage 7 (Figure 1D,E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figures 1D, 1E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Dl-/Dl- clones correctly transit into the endocycle.
source: These Dl-/Dl- clones also correctly transit into the endocycle, as their nuclear volumes are similar to wild-type follicle cells in the later stages of oogenesis after polyploidization (Figure 1F,G), whereas cells neighboring Dl-/Dl- follicle cell clones (retaining a cis-ligand but without a trans-ligand) are comparable to wild-type cells before entry to endocycle (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: Nuclear volumes of Dl-/Dl- clones are similar to wild-type follicle cells in the later stages of oogenesis after polyploidization.
source: These Dl-/Dl- clones also correctly transit into the endocycle, as their nuclear volumes are similar to wild-type follicle cells in the later stages of oogenesis after polyploidization (Figure 1F,G), whereas cells neighboring Dl-/Dl- follicle cell clones (retaining a cis-ligand but without a trans-ligand) are comparable to wild-type cells before entry to endocycle (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: Cells neighboring Dl-/Dl- follicle cell clones (retaining a cis-ligand but without a trans-ligand) are comparable to wild-type cells before entry to endocycle.
source: These Dl-/Dl- clones also correctly transit into the endocycle, as their nuclear volumes are similar to wild-type follicle cells in the later stages of oogenesis after polyploidization (Figure 1F,G), whereas cells neighboring Dl-/Dl- follicle cell clones (retaining a cis-ligand but without a trans-ligand) are comparable to wild-type cells before entry to endocycle (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: Removal of both cis- and trans-Dl through knockdown of Dl by RNA interference (RNAi) simultaneously in the germline and soma confirmed that follicle cells without both cis- and trans-ligand sources can still enter the endocycle stages of oogenesis.
source: Removal of both cis- and trans-Dl through knockdown of Dl by RNA interference (RNAi) simultaneously in the germline and soma confirmed this finding (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Follicle cells without both cis- and trans-ligand sources can still enter the endocycle stages of oogenesis.
source: Together, these observations provide evidence that follicle cells without both cis- and trans-ligand sources can still enter the endocycle stages of oogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The back-up route to the endocycle in Dl-/Dl- cells is not a co-option of Ser in place of Dl.
source: This back-up route to the endocycle is not a co-option of Ser in place of Dl, as DlRevF10SerRx82 double clones recapitulated the Dl-/Dl- phenotype (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: DlRevF10SerRx82 double clones recapitulated the Dl-/Dl- phenotype.
source: This back-up route to the endocycle is not a co-option of Ser in place of Dl, as DlRevF10SerRx82 double clones recapitulated the Dl-/Dl- phenotype (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Notch is required for the mitotic-to-endocycle switch in Dl-/Dl- follicle cells.
source: Dl-/Dl- clones driving expression of NotchRNAi show a significantly higher proportion (p < 0.0001) of late Cut-expressing cells than the Dl-/Dl- clones alone, indicating that Notch is still required for the mitotic-to-endocycle switch (Figures 1D and 2A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figures 1D, 2A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Dl-/Dl- clones driving expression of NotchRNAi show a significantly higher proportion (p < 0.0001) of late Cut-expressing cells than the Dl-/Dl- clones alone.
source: Dl-/Dl- clones driving expression of NotchRNAi show a significantly higher proportion (p < 0.0001) of late Cut-expressing cells than the Dl-/Dl- clones alone, indicating that Notch is still required for the mitotic-to-endocycle switch (Figures 1D and 2A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figures 1D, 2A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: MARCM clones for the null allele of Suppressor of Hairless, Su(H)47, in RNAi-induced Dl-/Dl- clones show late Cut expression (p < 0.0001).
source: Likewise, MARCM clones for the null allele of Suppressor of Hairless (Drosophila Notch transcriptional effector), Su(H)47, in RNAi-induced Dl-/Dl- clones also show late Cut expression (p < 0.0001) (Figure 2B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, Supplementary file 1) in comparison with RNAi-induced Dl/Dl- clone controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,D).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,D.

claim: A Notch activity reporter, Notch Responsive Element (NRE)-green fluorescent protein (GFP) was upregulated in Dl-/Dl- clones as early as stage 2.
source: A Notch activity reporter, Notch Responsive Element (NRE)-green fluorescent protein (GFP) (Stempfle et al., 2010) was also upregulated in Dl-/Dl- clones as early as stage 2, and this expression persisted beyond stage 6 (Figure 2C,D), suggesting that NRE-GFP is probably more sensitive to Notch activation than Hnt in follicle cells.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: NRE-GFP expression in Dl-/Dl- clones persisted beyond stage 6.
source: A Notch activity reporter, Notch Responsive Element (NRE)-green fluorescent protein (GFP) (Stempfle et al., 2010) was also upregulated in Dl-/Dl- clones as early as stage 2, and this expression persisted beyond stage 6 (Figure 2C,D), suggesting that NRE-GFP is probably more sensitive to Notch activation than Hnt in follicle cells.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: NRE-GFP is probably more sensitive to Notch activation than Hnt in follicle cells.
source: A Notch activity reporter, Notch Responsive Element (NRE)-green fluorescent protein (GFP) (Stempfle et al., 2010) was also upregulated in Dl-/Dl- clones as early as stage 2, and this expression persisted beyond stage 6 (Figure 2C,D), suggesting that NRE-GFP is probably more sensitive to Notch activation than Hnt in follicle cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Notch activity occurs independently of canonical ligands when both cis- and trans-ligands are removed, resulting in normal downstream developmental events in the follicle cells.
source: Together, these results suggest that Notch activity occurs independently of canonical ligands when both cis- and trans-ligands are removed, resulting in normal downstream developmental events in the follicle cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: DlRevF10SerRx82 double mutant clones in the wing and eye discs show a slight cell-autonomous upregulation of NRE-GFP in the clone center.
source: Consistently, DlRevF10SerRx82 double mutant clones in the wing and eye discs show a slight cell-autonomous upregulation of NRE-GFP in the clone center, which would only occur if cis-inhibition blocked a DSL-independent mode of Notch activity, as interior cells have no access to trans-ligand (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: Cell-autonomous upregulation of NRE-GFP in the clone center would only occur if cis-inhibition blocked a DSL-independent mode of Notch activity, as interior cells have no access to trans-ligand.
source: Consistently, DlRevF10SerRx82 double mutant clones in the wing and eye discs show a slight cell-autonomous upregulation of NRE-GFP in the clone center, which would only occur if cis-inhibition blocked a DSL-independent mode of Notch activity, as interior cells have no access to trans-ligand (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: NRE-GFP upregulation in wing disc clones was spatially variable, having the highest prevalence in the notum region (25% incidence).
source: This NRE-GFP upregulation was spatially variable in the wing disc, having the highest prevalence in the notum region (25% incidence), a low incidence in the dorsal pouch (8%), whereas in the ventral pouch region it was never seen (n = 80) (Supplementary file 1), perhaps owing to the differential regulation of Notch degradation throughout the wing disc (Hori et al., 2011).
evidence: This is experimental data reported in the text and Supplementary file 1.

claim: NRE-GFP upregulation in wing disc clones had a low incidence in the dorsal pouch (8%).
source: This NRE-GFP upregulation was spatially variable in the wing disc, having the highest prevalence in the notum region (25% incidence), a low incidence in the dorsal pouch (8%), whereas in the ventral pouch region it was never seen (n = 80) (Supplementary file 1), perhaps owing to the differential regulation of Notch degradation throughout the wing disc (Hori et al., 2011).
evidence: This is experimental data reported in the text and Supplementary file 1.

claim: NRE-GFP upregulation in wing disc clones was never seen in the ventral pouch region (n = 80).
source: This NRE-GFP upregulation was spatially variable in the wing disc, having the highest prevalence in the notum region (25% incidence), a low incidence in the dorsal pouch (8%), whereas in the ventral pouch region it was never seen (n = 80) (Supplementary file 1), perhaps owing to the differential regulation of Notch degradation throughout the wing disc (Hori et al., 2011).
evidence: This is experimental data reported in the text and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Spatial variability in NRE-GFP upregulation in wing disc clones is perhaps owing to the differential regulation of Notch degradation throughout the wing disc.
source: This NRE-GFP upregulation was spatially variable in the wing disc, having the highest prevalence in the notum region (25% incidence), a low incidence in the dorsal pouch (8%), whereas in the ventral pouch region it was never seen (n = 80) (Supplementary file 1), perhaps owing to the differential regulation of Notch degradation throughout the wing disc (Hori et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation.

claim: Most wing disc clones showed a higher NRE-GFP upregulation in the clone boundary where there is access to trans-ligand.
source: As reported previously, most wing disc clones showed a higher NRE-GFP upregulation in the clone boundary where there is access to trans-ligand, indicating that the ligand-independent Notch activity observed occurs at a rather low level.
evidence: This is experimental observation reported in the text.

claim: The ligand-independent Notch activity observed occurs at a rather low level.
source: As reported previously, most wing disc clones showed a higher NRE-GFP upregulation in the clone boundary where there is access to trans-ligand, indicating that the ligand-independent Notch activity observed occurs at a rather low level.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observation.

claim: Drosophila S2 cells have no Dl expression.
source: Drosophila S2 cells are reported to have no Dl expression and a very low level of Ser expression, which had no effect on Notch signaling (Fehon et al., 1990; Graveley et al., 2011) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and have been used as a model to study ligand-independent Notch activity (Hori et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and confirmed in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Drosophila S2 cells have a very low level of Ser expression, which had no effect on Notch signaling.
source: Drosophila S2 cells are reported to have no Dl expression and a very low level of Ser expression, which had no effect on Notch signaling (Fehon et al., 1990; Graveley et al., 2011) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and have been used as a model to study ligand-independent Notch activity (Hori et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and confirmed in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Drosophila S2 cells have been used as a model to study ligand-independent Notch activity.
source: Drosophila S2 cells are reported to have no Dl expression and a very low level of Ser expression, which had no effect on Notch signaling (Fehon et al., 1990; Graveley et al., 2011) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and have been used as a model to study ligand-independent Notch activity (Hori et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Upon transfection with pMT-NFL, Notch activation was increased by a factor of 5.13 compared with the control cells (p < 0.0001).
source: Upon transfection with pMT-NFL, a CuSO4-inducible full-length Notch construct, Notch activation was increased by a factor of 5.13 compared with the control cells, as indicated by a NRE-firefly luciferase reporter gene (p < 0.0001) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Notch activation in S2 cells is at least partially dependent on endosomal trafficking.
source: Notch activation in S2 cells is at least partially dependent on endosomal trafficking, as double-stranded (ds) RNA against early endosome component, Rab5, or multivesicular body sorting protein, hrs, reduced the levels of Notch activation (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: dsRNA against Rab5 reduced the levels of Notch activation in S2 cells (Rab5 p = 0.00623).
source: Notch activation in S2 cells is at least partially dependent on endosomal trafficking, as double-stranded (ds) RNA against early endosome component, Rab5, or multivesicular body sorting protein, hrs, reduced the levels of Notch activation (Figure 3A,B). This is consistent with the in vivo studies indicating that ligand-independent Notch activation relies heavily on receptor trafficking (Hori et al., 2012) (Rab5 p = 0.00623, hrs p = 0.0159), and our observation that Notch accumulates in Dl-/Dl- clones (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: dsRNA against hrs reduced the levels of Notch activation in S2 cells (hrs p = 0.0159).
source: Notch activation in S2 cells is at least partially dependent on endosomal trafficking, as double-stranded (ds) RNA against early endosome component, Rab5, or multivesicular body sorting protein, hrs, reduced the levels of Notch activation (Figure 3A,B). This is consistent with the in vivo studies indicating that ligand-independent Notch activation relies heavily on receptor trafficking (Hori et al., 2012) (Rab5 p = 0.00623, hrs p = 0.0159), and our observation that Notch accumulates in Dl-/Dl- clones (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Ligand-independent Notch activation relies heavily on receptor trafficking.
source: This is consistent with the in vivo studies indicating that ligand-independent Notch activation relies heavily on receptor trafficking (Hori et al., 2012) (Rab5 p = 0.00623, hrs p = 0.0159), and our observation that Notch accumulates in Dl-/Dl- clones (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation and consistent with the experimental data.

claim: Notch accumulates in Dl-/Dl- clones.
source: This is consistent with the in vivo studies indicating that ligand-independent Notch activation relies heavily on receptor trafficking (Hori et al., 2012) (Rab5 p = 0.00623, hrs p = 0.0159), and our observation that Notch accumulates in Dl-/Dl- clones (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: A requirement for trafficking is consistent with the results of others who have demonstrated aberrant Notch activation in follicle cell mutants for trafficking components.
source: A requirement for trafficking is consistent with the results of others who have demonstrated aberrant Notch activation in follicle cell mutants for trafficking components (Wilkin et al., 2004; Vaccari et al., 2008; Schneider et al., 2013), such as tsg101 mutant clones, which show early Notch activation in the follicle cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and consistent with the experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: tsg101 mutant clones show early Notch activation in the follicle cells.
source: A requirement for trafficking is consistent with the results of others who have demonstrated aberrant Notch activation in follicle cell mutants for trafficking components (Wilkin et al., 2004; Vaccari et al., 2008; Schneider et al., 2013), such as tsg101 mutant clones, which show early Notch activation in the follicle cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Co-transfecting pMT-NFL with pMT-GAL4 and pUASt-Serdel3 almost entirely abolished the Notch activation detected when NFL was transfected alone (p = 0.0048).
source: Furthermore, co-transfecting pMT-NFL with pMT-GAL4 and pUASt-Serdel3, a form of Ser that cannot activate Notch, but only cis-inhibit, (Fleming et al., 2013) almost entirely abolished the Notch activation detected when NFL was transfected alone (p = 0.0048) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Serdel3 is a form of Ser that cannot activate Notch, but only cis-inhibit.
source: Furthermore, co-transfecting pMT-NFL with pMT-GAL4 and pUASt-Serdel3, a form of Ser that cannot activate Notch, but only cis-inhibit, (Fleming et al., 2013) almost entirely abolished the Notch activation detected when NFL was transfected alone (p = 0.0048) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: If Notch is expressed in a cell free of cis- and trans-ligands, DSL ligand-independent activity will occur.
source: These results suggest that if Notch is expressed in a cell free of cis- and trans-ligands, DSL ligand-independent activity will occur and that cis-inhibition is extremely efficient in preventing this 'accidental' Notch activity as it travels through the endosomal pathway en route to degradation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Cis-inhibition is extremely efficient in preventing 'accidental' Notch activity as it travels through the endosomal pathway en route to degradation.
source: These results suggest that if Notch is expressed in a cell free of cis- and trans-ligands, DSL ligand-independent activity will occur and that cis-inhibition is extremely efficient in preventing this 'accidental' Notch activity as it travels through the endosomal pathway en route to degradation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Wingless (Wg) is normally expressed along the dorsoventral boundary of the wing disc.
source: The Notch target, Wingless (Wg) is normally expressed along the dorsoventral boundary of the wing disc (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is established knowledge shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Lethal giant disc (lgd) homozygous mutant (lgdd7) larvae display overgrown imaginal discs.
source: Lethal giant disc (lgd) homozygous mutant (lgdd7) larvae display overgrown imaginal discs and ubiquitous ligand-independent Notch activation in the wing pouch region, as shown by upregulation of Wg (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Lethal giant disc (lgd) homozygous mutant (lgdd7) larvae display ubiquitous ligand-independent Notch activation in the wing pouch region, as shown by upregulation of Wg.
source: Lethal giant disc (lgd) homozygous mutant (lgdd7) larvae display overgrown imaginal discs and ubiquitous ligand-independent Notch activation in the wing pouch region, as shown by upregulation of Wg (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Notch activation in lgd mutant cells is caused by a defect in Notch trafficking and degradation.
source: Notch activation in lgd mutant cells is caused by a defect in Notch trafficking and degradation, as the receptor is aberrantly transported to the limiting membrane of the lysosome which facilitates production of NICD (Childress et al., 2006; Gallagher and Knoblich, 2006; Jaekel and Klein, 2006; Schneider et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In lgd mutant cells, the Notch receptor is aberrantly transported to the limiting membrane of the lysosome which facilitates production of NICD.
source: Notch activation in lgd mutant cells is caused by a defect in Notch trafficking and degradation, as the receptor is aberrantly transported to the limiting membrane of the lysosome which facilitates production of NICD (Childress et al., 2006; Gallagher and Knoblich, 2006; Jaekel and Klein, 2006; Schneider et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Using dpp-GAL4 to misexpress UAS-Dl along the anterior–posterior axis of the wing disc in lgdd7 homozygous larvae, Wg expression was considerably reduced along the dpp expression domain.
source: Using dpp-GAL4 to misexpress UAS-Dl along the anterior–posterior axis of the wing disc in lgdd7 homozygous larvae, Wg expression was considerably reduced along the dpp expression domain, indicating that cis-inhibition can block the ligand-independent Notch activity observed in this situation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Cis-inhibition can block the ligand-independent Notch activity observed in lgd mutant cells.
source: Using dpp-GAL4 to misexpress UAS-Dl along the anterior–posterior axis of the wing disc in lgdd7 homozygous larvae, Wg expression was considerably reduced along the dpp expression domain, indicating that cis-inhibition can block the ligand-independent Notch activity observed in this situation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Overexpression of Deltex (Dx) induces ligand-independent Notch activation specifically in the ventral wing pouch region.
source: Overexpression of Deltex (Dx), an E3 ubiquitin ligase that stimulates Notch monoubiquitination and promotes its trafficking to the lysosomal limiting membrane, has also been shown to induce ligand-independent Notch activation specifically in the ventral wing pouch region (Matsuno et al., 2002; Hori et al., 2004; Wilkin et al., 2008; Schneider et al., 2013) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Deltex (Dx) is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that stimulates Notch monoubiquitination and promotes its trafficking to the lysosomal limiting membrane.
source: Overexpression of Deltex (Dx), an E3 ubiquitin ligase that stimulates Notch monoubiquitination and promotes its trafficking to the lysosomal limiting membrane, has also been shown to induce ligand-independent Notch activation specifically in the ventral wing pouch region (Matsuno et al., 2002; Hori et al., 2004; Wilkin et al., 2008; Schneider et al., 2013) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Ectopic expression of UAS-Dl leads to a reduction of Wg staining along the dorsoventral boundary.
source: We used patched (ptc)-GAL4 to drive expression of UAS-Dx with either UAS-Dl or UAS-Serdel3, whose ectopic expression leads to a reduction of Wg staining along the dorsoventral boundary (Micchelli et al., 1997; Fleming et al., 2013) (controls in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,E).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,E.

claim: Ectopic expression of UAS-Serdel3 leads to a reduction of Wg staining along the dorsoventral boundary.
source: We used patched (ptc)-GAL4 to drive expression of UAS-Dx with either UAS-Dl or UAS-Serdel3, whose ectopic expression leads to a reduction of Wg staining along the dorsoventral boundary (Micchelli et al., 1997; Fleming et al., 2013) (controls in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,E).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,E.

claim: Co-expression of Dx and Dl led to a decrease in Wg expression in the ventral ptc domain as compared with expression of Dx alone.
source: Co-expression of Dx and Dl led to a decrease in Wg expression in the ventral ptc domain as compared with expression of Dx alone (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: When UAS-Dx and UAS-Serdel3 were co-expressed, there was a small but noticeable, albeit variable, decrease in Dx-induced Notch activation.
source: When UAS-Dx and UAS-Serdel3 were co-expressed, there was a small but noticeable, albeit variable, decrease in Dx-induced Notch activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: The incomplete reduction of Dx-induced Notch activation by UAS-Serdel3 was probably due to the previously noted, slightly compromised, cis-inhibitory potential of UAS-Serdel3.
source: This incomplete reduction was probably due to the previously noted, slightly compromised, cis-inhibitory potential of UAS-Serdel3 (Fleming et al., 2013) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Cis-ligand has a negative effect on the raised levels of DSL-ligand independent Notch activation incurred in genetically abnormal cells.
source: Taken together, these results provide evidence that cis-ligand has a negative effect on the raised levels of DSL-ligand independent Notch activation incurred in genetically abnormal cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Co-transfection with pMT-NFL and pMT-Dx caused an increase by a factor of 4.21 (p = 0.0021) in the Notch activation compared with transfecting pMT-NFL alone.
source: To quantify this effect, we co-transfected pMT-Dx with pMT-NFL, causing an increase by a factor of 4.21 (p = 0.0021) in the Notch activation compared with transfecting pMT-NFL alone (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Transfection of pMT-NFL, pMT-Dx, pMT-GAL4, and pUASt-Serdel3 significantly (p = 0.0194) reduced the level of Notch activation compared to pMT-NFL and pMT-Dx alone.
source: Transfection of pMT-NFL, pMT-Dx, pMT-GAL4, and pUASt-Serdel3 significantly (p = 0.0194) reduced the level of Notch activation (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Lgd dsRNA induced an increase in Notch activation by a factor of 1.73 compared with GFP dsRNA-treated cells (p = 0.00286).
source: We next treated cells with dsRNA for either lgd or shrub (a component of the ESCRT-III complex). Lgd dsRNA induced an increase in Notch activation by a factor of 1.73 compared with GFP dsRNA-treated cells (p = 0.00286) (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Shrub dsRNA caused a 3.93-fold increase (p < 0.0001) in Notch activation in S2 cells.
source: Likewise, shrub dsRNA caused a 3.93-fold increase (p < 0.0001) in Notch activation in S2 cells (Figure 4H) (Thompson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Expression of Serdel3 in lgd dsRNA-treated cells led to a significant decrease (p = 0.0093) in the amount of Notch activated in comparison with Notch-expressing cells treated with control dsRNA.
source: Expression of Serdel3 in both situations led to a significant decrease in the amount of Notch activated in comparison with Notch-expressing cells treated with control dsRNA (lgd p = 0.0093, shrub p = 0.0257) (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Expression of Serdel3 in shrub dsRNA-treated cells led to a significant decrease (p = 0.0257) in the amount of Notch activated in comparison with Notch-expressing cells treated with control dsRNA.
source: Expression of Serdel3 in both situations led to a significant decrease in the amount of Notch activated in comparison with Notch-expressing cells treated with control dsRNA (lgd p = 0.0093, shrub p = 0.0257) (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Crystal cells in the larval lymph gland have ligand-independent Notch activation.
source: To explore whether cis-acting ligands might block endogenous raised levels of ligand-independent Notch activation, in addition to the raised levels induced by genetic defects, we examined the effect of increased ligand expression in crystal cells in the larval lymph gland, which have recently been shown to have ligand-independent Notch activation (Mukherjee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Notch activity in crystal cells promotes cell survival.
source: Notch activity in crystal cells promotes cell survival, and decreased Notch activity leads to a 'bursting' phenotype (Mukherjee et al., 2011) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,E).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,E.

claim: Decreased Notch activity in crystal cells leads to a 'bursting' phenotype.
source: Notch activity in crystal cells promotes cell survival, and decreased Notch activity leads to a 'bursting' phenotype (Mukherjee et al., 2011) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,E).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,E.

claim: Using Lz-GAL4 to misexpress UAS-NotchRNAi led to a significantly higher proportion of cells showing the 'bursting' phenotype than wild-type crystal cells (p = 0.0434).
source: Using Lozenge (Lz)-GAL4, a crystal cell lineage-specific driver (Terriente-Felix et al., 2013) to misexpress UAS-NotchRNAi or UAS-Serdel3 led to a significantly higher proportion of cells showed the 'bursting' phenotype than wild-type crystal cells (NotchRNAi p = 0.0434, Serdel3 p = 0.0286) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B,E).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B,E.

claim: Using Lz-GAL4 to misexpress UAS-Serdel3 led to a significantly higher proportion of cells showing the 'bursting' phenotype than wild-type crystal cells (p = 0.0286).
source: Using Lozenge (Lz)-GAL4, a crystal cell lineage-specific driver (Terriente-Felix et al., 2013) to misexpress UAS-NotchRNAi or UAS-Serdel3 led to a significantly higher proportion of cells showed the 'bursting' phenotype than wild-type crystal cells (NotchRNAi p = 0.0434, Serdel3 p = 0.0286) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B,E).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B,E.

claim: Overexpression of UAS-SerWT led to a significant decrease of the Notch reporter E(spl):mβ-CD2 expression in mature crystal cells.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of UAS-SerWT led to a significant decrease of the Notch reporter E(spl):mβ-CD2expression in mature crystal cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D,F).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D,F.

claim: Reduced Notch reporter activity in crystal cells was not caused by indirect effects on early ligand-dependent Notch signaling in prohaemocytes.
source: Reduced Notch reporter activity was not caused by indirect effects on early ligand-dependent Notch signaling in prohaemocytes, as Hnt, a Notch target in differentiating crystal cells, (Terriente-Felix et al., 2013) was unaffected by ligand misexpression (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: Hnt is a Notch target in differentiating crystal cells.
source: Reduced Notch reporter activity was not caused by indirect effects on early ligand-dependent Notch signaling in prohaemocytes, as Hnt, a Notch target in differentiating crystal cells, (Terriente-Felix et al., 2013) was unaffected by ligand misexpression (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Increased ligand expression in crystal cells decreases cell survival by blocking Notch ligand-independent activation.
source: These observations indicate that increased ligand expression in crystal cells decreases cell survival by blocking Notch ligand-independent activation, and therefore the buffering role of cis-expressed ligand can be extended to endogenous cases of DSL-independent Notch activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The buffering role of cis-expressed ligand can be extended to endogenous cases of DSL-independent Notch activity.
source: These observations indicate that increased ligand expression in crystal cells decreases cell survival by blocking Notch ligand-independent activation, and therefore the buffering role of cis-expressed ligand can be extended to endogenous cases of DSL-independent Notch activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cells devoid of DSL ligands activate Notch sufficiently to stimulate reporter activity.
source: In this study, we show that cells devoid of DSL ligands activate Notch sufficiently to stimulate reporter activity, and in the ovarian follicle cells the level of activation is above the threshold required to mediate normal Notch-induced downstream developmental events.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: In the ovarian follicle cells, the level of Notch activation in cells devoid of DSL ligands is above the threshold required to mediate normal Notch-induced downstream developmental events.
source: In this study, we show that cells devoid of DSL ligands activate Notch sufficiently to stimulate reporter activity, and in the ovarian follicle cells the level of activation is above the threshold required to mediate normal Notch-induced downstream developmental events.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: During development, noncanonical Notch activity is normally prevented by cis-expressed DSL ligands in numerous tissues.
source: During development, this type of noncanonical Notch activity is normally prevented by cis-expressed DSL ligands in numerous tissues.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Cis-inhibition can attenuate DSL-ligand independent Notch activity both in endogenous and genetically induced situations.
source: Cis-inhibition can also attenuate DSL-ligand independent Notch activity both in endogenous and genetically induced situations.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: DSL ligands might sequester Notch at the membrane.
source: Mechanistically, this could be explained if DSL ligands sequestered Notch at the membrane, made Notch more sensitive to degradation, or increased the stability of the heterodimer as it travels through the endosomal pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation for the observed effects.

claim: DSL ligands might make Notch more sensitive to degradation.
source: Mechanistically, this could be explained if DSL ligands sequestered Notch at the membrane, made Notch more sensitive to degradation, or increased the stability of the heterodimer as it travels through the endosomal pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation for the observed effects.

claim: DSL ligands might increase the stability of the Notch heterodimer as it travels through the endosomal pathway.
source: Mechanistically, this could be explained if DSL ligands sequestered Notch at the membrane, made Notch more sensitive to degradation, or increased the stability of the heterodimer as it travels through the endosomal pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation for the observed effects.

claim: Increasing or decreasing ligand has variable effects on receptor distribution among tissues.
source: As we and others (Fiuza et al., 2010) have shown that increasing or decreasing ligand has variable effects on receptor distribution among tissues, and given that we observe a consistent effect among tissues on Notch activation upon cis-ligand removal, we prefer the stability hypothesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and supported by a citation.

claim: There is a consistent effect among tissues on Notch activation upon cis-ligand removal.
source: As we and others (Fiuza et al., 2010) have shown that increasing or decreasing ligand has variable effects on receptor distribution among tissues, and given that we observe a consistent effect among tissues on Notch activation upon cis-ligand removal, we prefer the stability hypothesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The stability hypothesis is the preferred mechanistic explanation for cis-inhibition effects.
source: As we and others (Fiuza et al., 2010) have shown that increasing or decreasing ligand has variable effects on receptor distribution among tissues, and given that we observe a consistent effect among tissues on Notch activation upon cis-ligand removal, we prefer the stability hypothesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and reasoning.

claim: Ligand affects Notch stability during Notch activation by EDTA.
source: Fiuza et al. (2010) show that ligand affects Notch stability during Notch activation by EDTA, giving support to the stability hypothesis as the most parsimonious explanation (Fiuza et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Retaining a pool of translated Notch receptor keeps the pathway in a condition capable of almost instant activation.
source: It is suggested that retaining a pool of translated Notch receptor keeps the pathway in a condition capable of almost instant activation (Sprinzak et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: A role of cis-ligands might be to keep the Notch pathway in a state of readiness by buffering against unintentional stochastic Notch activity resulting from normal processing through the endosomes.
source: Therefore, we propose that a role of cis-ligands might be to keep the Notch pathway in a state of readiness by buffering against unintentional stochastic Notch activity resulting from normal processing through the endosomes.
evidence: This is a proposed function based on the experimental findings and reasoning.

claim: Buffering against unintentional stochastic Notch activity may aid the ability of a cell to mediate future Notch-dependent developmental events that have strict temporal regulation.
source: Endogenously, this may aid the ability of a cell to mediate future Notch-dependent developmental events that have strict temporal regulation.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the proposed function of cis-inhibition.
